lesson.title: Storing Charge Between Two Plates: Meet the Capacitor
lesson.summary: A capacitor is two conductive plates separated by an insulating gap that store equal and opposite charge whenever a voltage is applied across them.
lesson.body:
Strip away the packaging and every capacitor is the same simple idea: two conductive plates facing each other, separated by a thin gap filled with an insulating material. On a schematic, that structure is drawn almost literally, as two parallel lines with a small gap between them, or for polarized types like electrolytic capacitors, one straight line and one curved line to mark which lead must stay positive. Unlike a resistor, which lets charge flow steadily through it, a capacitor's insulating gap blocks charge from crossing directly. Instead, it stores charge on its two separated plates.

Here is the mechanism, and it connects directly to two ideas you already have: electric charge and voltage. Connect a capacitor to a voltage source, and the source pushes electrons onto one plate, giving it a surplus of negative charge, while pulling electrons off the other plate, leaving it with a matching surplus of positive charge. No charge actually crosses the gap between the plates, but the buildup of opposite charges on the two plates creates an electric field across that gap, and that field corresponds to a voltage difference between the plates that grows to match the voltage of the source driving it. The capacitor is, in effect, a tiny reservoir where equal and opposite charge accumulates in response to an applied voltage.

The amount of charge a capacitor holds for a given voltage is described by a single number, its capacitance, measured in farads, and the relationship is Q equals C times V, where Q is the stored charge in coulombs, C is the capacitance in farads, and V is the voltage across the plates. The next chapter digs into what determines a capacitor's capacitance value, but the relationship itself is worth previewing here with real numbers.

Suppose a 100 microfarad capacitor, a very common size found in power supply filtering, is charged up to 5 volts. The stored charge is Q equals C times V, so Q equals 100 times 10 to the negative sixth farads, multiplied by 5 volts, which works out to 500 times 10 to the negative sixth coulombs, or 500 microcoulombs. Disconnect the source and that charge, and the voltage it represents, remains on the plates until something gives it a path to flow away, which is exactly why a charged capacitor can still deliver a jolt even after power is removed.

Because a capacitor blocks the direct flow of charge through its gap, it behaves very differently from a resistor when voltages change over time. A steady, unchanging DC voltage eventually leaves a capacitor fully charged and drawing no further current, effectively acting like an open switch. A voltage that keeps changing, however, keeps pushing charge on and off the plates, letting a capacitor pass along changing signals even though nothing physically crosses the gap. That charging and discharging behavior, and the timing that governs it, is a story for later chapters, but it starts with the simple physical picture built here: two plates, a gap, and charge pushed on by voltage.
